chunks.content: Introduction Bronchiectasis is a chronic pulmonary condition characterised by irreversible bronchial dilatation, impaired mucociliary clearance and recurrent exacerbations, associated with chronic inflammation and structural lung damage [ , ]. While patients may experience symptoms during clinical stability, such as persistent cough and purulent sputum production, exacerbations are defined as a deterioration in three or more key symptoms lasting at least 48 h, for which a clinician determines that a change in bronchiectasis treatment is required [ , ]. Bronchiectasis is a heterogeneous condition in terms of aetiology, as it may be associated with immune deficiencies, airway obstruction or prior pulmonary infections, as well as with genetic disorders such as cystic fibrosis (CF), alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency and primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) [ – ]. Nonetheless, in a substantial proportion of cases the underlying cause remains unknown, with idiopathic bronchiectasis accounting for ∼20–40% of cases across major international registries [ – ]. The prevalence of bronchiectasis has increased in recent years, owing to advances in diagnostic imaging and greater awareness among healthcare professionals [ , ]. This increased recognition may bring additional economic costs to healthcare systems, as more patients are identified and managed over time, although the underlying burden largely stems from frequent hospitalisations, chronic antibiotic use and impaired quality of life [ – ]. At the core of bronchiectasis pathophysiology lies a self-perpetuating cycle, commonly referred to as the “vicious vortex”, in which chronic inflammation leads to airway remodelling, impaired mucociliary clearance and persistent bacterial infection [ ]. In this cycle, bacterial pathogens are not merely bystanders but active contributors that amplify airway inflammation and disease progression [ ]. Among the most frequently isolated bacteria in bronchiectasis, Staphylococcus aureus , including both methicillin-sensitive (MSSA) and methicillin-resistant (MRSA) strains, is emerging as a clinically relevant pathogen. European data report S. aureus isolation in up to 13% of cases, less frequently than Pseudomonas aeruginosa (25.1%) or Haemophilus influenzae (23.6%), yet its role in severe disease and multidrug-resistant (MDR) infections is increasingly recognised [ , ]. S. aureus is a Gram-positive bacterium capable of persisting in the airways and causing disease through a range of virulence mechanisms [ , ]. These include epithelial invasion, toxin production, biofilm formation and immune evasion strategies, such as secretion of proteins that inhibit phagocytosis, neutralisation of antimicrobial peptides and intracellular persistence within host cells [ – ]. MRSA further complicates management due to its resistance to multiple antibiotic classes, limiting therapeutic options and potentially leading to worse clinical outcomes [ , ]. Recent bronchiectasis guidelines recommend eradication strategies for P. aeruginosa , but provide no specific recommendations regarding the management of S. aureus [ , ]. Furthermore, the interplay between S. aureus and other pathogens, including viruses, fungi and bacteria such as P. aeruginosa , adds further complexity to airway microbiome dynamics, with potential implications for disease progression and therapeutic approaches. In this review, we examine the impact of S. aureus on the pathophysiology and clinical course of bronchiectasis in adult patients. We explore its pathogenicity within the lungs, interactions with the host immune system, global epidemiology, and available strategies for treatment and prevention. By drawing comparisons with other chronic respiratory diseases when informative, we aim to enhance our understanding and identify knowledge gaps, particularly where disease-specific evidence is limited. Ultimately, we seek to highlight priorities for future research and practical considerations to support more effective clinical management of S. aureus in bronchiectasis. Methods This narrative review was conducted through a comprehensive search of the PubMed and Google Scholar electronic databases. The search included the keywords “bronchiectasis”, “ Staphylococcus aureus ”, “MRSA”, “chronic respiratory diseases”, “treatment” and “prevention”. Relevant studies were selected based on their clinical significance, methodological quality and relevance to the topic. The aim was to provide a balanced and comprehensive overview, integrating data from epidemiological studies, clinical trials and basic research to capture the full spectrum of S. aureus pathophysiology, clinical impact and management in bronchiectasis. Overview of <italic toggle="yes">S. aureus</italic> S. aureus is a facultative anaerobic, non-motile, non-spore-forming, coagulase-positive Gram-positive coccus [ , ]. It is regarded both as a commensal organism and a major human pathogen capable of causing a wide spectrum of infections, ranging from superficial skin infections to severe, life-threatening conditions such as pneumonia and septic shock [ , ]. S. aureus colonises the skin and gut, and is found in the anterior nares of ∼30% of individuals [ , ]. Its success as a human pathogen is attributed to a variety of factors, including its adaptability to diverse environments, genetic plasticity, extensive arsenal of toxins, and ability to evade and exploit host immune responses [ ]. From a respiratory perspective, S. aureus is associated with a broad spectrum of clinical manifestations, ranging from asymptomatic nasal carriage to severe necrotising pneumonia. Its success as a human pathogen is attributed to a variety of factors, including its adaptability to diverse environments, genetic plasticity, extensive arsenal of toxins, and ability to evade and exploit host immune responses [ ]. From a respiratory perspective, S. aureus is associated with a broad spectrum of clinical manifestations, ranging from asymptomatic nasal carriage to severe necrotising pneumonia. In the context of bronchiectasis, chronic inflammation, mucus stasis and lung damage may create a permissive environment that facilitates S. aureus persistence and colonisation within the airways. Oropharyngeal colonisation often represents the first step and is a well-established risk factor for pleuropulmonary infections, as aspiration into the lungs may result in invasive disease [ – , ]. The respiratory system is equipped with multiple defence mechanisms against bacterial invasion, including the airway and alveolar epithelium, and resident immune cells such as macrophages and neutrophils. S. aureus adheres to the respiratory epithelium and extracellular matrix via a variety of cell wall-anchored proteins known as MSCRAMMs (microbial surface components recognising adhesive matrix molecules) [ – ]. As illustrated in , S. aureus utilises a wide array of virulence mechanisms to evade host defences and establish persistent airway infection. First, it secretes a range of pore-forming cytolytic toxins that destroy immune cells such as macrophages and neutrophils. Key toxins include α- and β-toxin, phenol-soluble modulins and Panton–Valentine leukocidin (PVL) [ – ]. These toxins contribute to parenchymal damage and inflammation; PVL, in particular, is associated with massive neutrophilic influx into the lungs and the formation of microabscesses, which are hallmark features of S. aureus pneumonia [ – ]. Second, S. aureus deploys mechanical defences, including a dense polysaccharide capsule and biofilm formation, which enhance its persistence in the airways and its ability to evade immune detection [ – ]. Over 90% of S. aureus isolates produce a capsular polysaccharide that inhibits complement opsonisation and protects the bacterium from phagocytosis [ ]. Furthermore, biofilms, composed of exopolysaccharides, extracellular DNA, teichoic acids and proteins, form robust protective barriers that provide structural stability, shield S. aureus from immune responses and limit antibiotic penetration. Biofilm formation plays a critical role in the bacterium's persistence in chronic respiratory diseases, particularly in conditions such as chronic rhinosinusitis and CF, although its role in bronchiectasis remains less well defined [ , ]. Another feature that enables S. aureus to survive and persist in the respiratory system is its capacity to switch to the small colony variant (SCV) phenotype. SCVs are a distinct, slow-growing form of S. aureus that play a significant role in its pathogenesis in chronic lung diseases. They are characterised by reduced toxin production, altered metabolism, and increased resistance to oxidative stress and antibiotic pressure, allowing them to survive in hostile environments and evade the host immune response [ ]. In addition, S. aureus can elicit an exaggerated immune response through the production of superantigens, which, unlike conventional antigens, do not require processing by antigen-presenting cells to activate T-lymphocytes [ ]. Another key pathogenic feature of S. aureus is its ability to develop antibiotic resistance. Most methicillin-sensitive S. aureus strains produce BlaZ penicillinase, an enzyme that hydrolyses penicillin and aminopenicillins ( e.g. ampicillin and amoxicillin), unless combined with a β-lactamase inhibitor such as clavulanic acid. Nevertheless, BlaZ-producing MSSA remains susceptible to anti-staphylococcal β-lactams, including oxacillin and cefazolin, because these agents are structurally resistant to hydrolysis by the BlaZ β-lactamase [ , ]. Furthermore, MSSA may harbour additional acquired resistance to macrolides, lincosamides, fluoroquinolones and tetracyclines. These mechanisms are mediated by horizontally acquired genes ( e.g. erm , msrA , tetK and tetM ) and chromosomal mutations ( e.g. in gyrA and parC ) [ ]. Recent metagenomic studies have characterised the S. aureus resistome (the full complement of antibiotic resistance genes), revealing a broad repertoire even when S. aureus is present at low abundance in respiratory samples. These approaches may overcome some limitations of conventional culture-based susceptibility testing [ , ]. MRSA has spread rapidly across the globe. Hospital-acquired MRSA is now endemic in most healthcare settings, with a prevalence exceeding 30–50% of S. aureus hospital isolates in many countries [ ]. Community-acquired MRSA clones are also increasingly detected both in the community and in healthcare environments. For instance, a US study reported a 10-fold higher incidence of community-acquired MRSA compared to hospital-acquired MRSA (316 versus 31 cases per 100 000 population) [ ]. This resistance is conferred by the mecA gene, which encodes an altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a) with markedly reduced affinity for most β-lactams. Community-acquired MRSA clones are also increasingly detected both in the community and in healthcare environments. For instance, a US study reported a 10-fold higher incidence of community-acquired MRSA compared to hospital-acquired MRSA (316 versus 31 cases per 100 000 population) [ ]. This resistance is conferred by the mecA gene, which encodes an altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a) with markedly reduced affinity for most β-lactams. The mecA gene is located on the staphylococcal cassette chromosome mec (SCC mec ), a mobile genetic element (MGE) believed to have been acquired horizontally from coagulase-negative staphylococci [ , ]. The versatility of MGEs, such as SCC mec , plays a critical role in the adaptability and pathogenicity of S. aureus . These elements facilitate horizontal gene transfer and carry genes that contribute to antibiotic resistance, biofilm formation and the production of multiple toxins [ ]. Consequently, treatment of S. aureus lung infections largely depends on its susceptibility profile. For MSSA, β-lactam antibiotics such as oxacillin or cefazolin are the preferred options. In the case of MRSA, alternative therapies are required. Linezolid and vancomycin are possible options, while fifth-generation cephalosporins offer a valuable β-lactam choice due to their activity against PBP2a, making them suitable for severe scenarios [ , ]. Oral bioavailable drugs such as amoxicillin–clavulanate, trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole and doxycycline can be considered for milder cases [ ]. Daptomycin, although effective against MRSA, is not suitable for lung infections due to its inactivation by pulmonary surfactant. Taken together, these virulence and resistance mechanisms, when combined with bronchiectasis impaired airway defences, may enhance S. aureus survival and pathogenicity, ultimately contributing to its persistence and clinical impact in affected lungs. The role of <italic toggle="yes">S. aureus</italic> in other chronic lung diseases Asthma In asthma and chronic rhinosinusitis, S. aureus is closely associated with severe, late-onset, non-atopic phenotypes of the disease [ , ]. Some of its virulence factors, particularly staphylococcal enterotoxins, function as superantigens capable of bypassing conventional antigen processing and triggering a type 2 (T2) immune response [ , , ]. This leads to the secretion of cytokines such as interleukin (IL)-4, IL-5 and IL-13, which play key roles in promoting eosinophilic inflammation and mucus hypersecretion [ ]. Furthermore, S. aureus stimulates airway epithelial cells to release alarmins ( e.g. thymic stromal lymphopoietin and IL-33), which further amplify the T2 inflammatory cascade [ ]. The presence of specific IgE to staphylococcal enterotoxin in patients correlates with disease severity, frequent hospitalisations and corticosteroid dependence, underscoring the potential utility of targeted therapies such as anti-IgE agents [ , ]. COPD S. aureus has historically been considered an infrequent and low-impact pathogen in COPD. Although it can be isolated during exacerbations, its role in disease progression and acute deterioration remains less well defined. Pathogens such as H. influenzae , Moraxella catarrhalis and P. aeruginosa are more consistently linked to clinical impact in both stable disease and exacerbations [ , ]. However, emerging evidence suggests that S. aureus may sustain chronic inflammation and lung function decline in COPD. Colonisation of the lower airways is associated with immune dysregulation, as shown by elevated IgE antibodies against staphylococcal enterotoxins in both stable and exacerbated COPD patients [ , ]. Notably, a reduction in these IgE levels during acute exacerbations is associated with improved lung function, suggesting a role for S. aureus superantigens in triggering inflammatory responses [ , ]. Beyond immune activation and T2 inflammation, S. aureus may contribute to COPD progression through metabolic dysregulation and neutrophilic inflammation. A recent translational study from China showed that S. aureus colonisation increases airway homocysteine, promoting NETosis (neutrophil extracellular trap formation) over apoptosis in neutrophils, thereby also sustaining neutrophilic inflammation [ ]. Regarding MRSA, a retrospective study of 160 patients hospitalised for acute COPD exacerbations found nasal carriage in 20.6% of cases, which was associated with more frequent prior hospitalisations and worse in-hospital outcomes, including longer stays, greater antibiotic exposure and increased need for non-invasive ventilation or intensive care unit (ICU) care, despite similar mortality rates [ ]. CF and PCD In CF, S. aureus is one of the earliest airway colonisers, with prevalence rates up to 80% in children aged 6–17 years and remaining substantial (40–50%) in adults [ , ]. Chronic S. aureus infection, particularly MRSA, is associated with accelerated lung function decline, increased hospitalisations and overall higher morbidity [ ]. Thanks to its biofilm formation and broad virulence repertoire, S. aureus disrupts epithelial integrity and elicits strong immune responses, fostering a pro-inflammatory environment. Some countries, such as the UK, recommend anti- S. aureus antibiotics for primary prophylaxis, although this approach is not universally adopted. Targeted antibiotics are also used to manage exacerbations [ , ]. Frequent anti-staphylococcal antibiotic therapy, together with the inflammation induced by S. aureus ,

Chronic S. aureus infection, particularly MRSA, is associated with accelerated lung function decline, increased hospitalisations and overall higher morbidity [ ]. Thanks to its biofilm formation and broad virulence repertoire, S. aureus disrupts epithelial integrity and elicits strong immune responses, fostering a pro-inflammatory environment. Some countries, such as the UK, recommend anti- S. aureus antibiotics for primary prophylaxis, although this approach is not universally adopted. Targeted antibiotics are also used to manage exacerbations [ , ]. Frequent anti-staphylococcal antibiotic therapy, together with the inflammation induced by S. aureus , may not only cause direct lung damage but also create conditions that favour secondary infection by P. aeruginosa , a transition associated with further clinical deterioration [ ]. This concern, eradicating S. aureus potentially promoting P. aeruginosa dominance, may also be relevant in bronchiectasis. In contrast, S. aureus colonisation in PCD follows a different pattern. Studies indicate that ∼34% of PCD patients are colonised by S. aureus , with prevalence rates of ∼31% in children and ∼40% in adults [ ]. Unlike in CF, S. aureus does not appear to significantly impact lung function in PCD, and P. aeruginosa becomes the dominant pathogen in adulthood [ ]. Consequently, treatment in PCD typically focuses on symptom control without specific eradication protocols for S. aureus as occurs in bronchiectasis. The role of <italic toggle="yes">S. aureus</italic> in bronchiectasis Prevalence and differences in geographic distribution S. aureus is less frequently isolated in bronchiectasis compared to other respiratory pathogens. Epidemiological data indicate that its prevalence in sputum samples is lower than that of P. aeruginosa and H. influenzae , with notable regional variation ( ). The European Multicentre Bronchiectasis Audit and Research Collaboration (EMBARC) registry reported a prevalence of S. aureus of 8.6%, with higher rates observed in Northern and Western European countries (13%) [ ]. Similarly, the US Bronchiectasis Research Registry found a slightly higher overall prevalence of 12% [ ]. Much lower rates have been recorded in Asia, with S. aureus isolated in only 1.1% of cases in China and 0.7% in Korea, while the Australian Bronchiectasis Registry reports an intermediate prevalence of 5% [ , , ]. Data from the Spanish Bronchiectasis Registry (RIBRON) reported a prevalence of S. aureus isolation of 7.6%, with 7.5% of patients meeting the criteria for chronic infection. Of these, 0.3% had chronic infection with MRSA, highlighting the relatively low prevalence of MRSA even among chronically infected patients [ ]. Data on MRSA are even more limited in other regions. In a large retrospective cohort of bronchiectasis patients in Taiwan, among 554 individuals with MDR bacterial infections, MRSA was the second most common MDR pathogen, affecting 18.4% of cases [ ]. However, considering that the study included over 8000 bronchiectasis patients with available sputum cultures, the overall prevalence of MRSA within the entire cohort was substantially lower, reflecting a similar trend to the RIBRON data. Differences in S. aureus prevalence across bronchiectasis registries may likely reflect a combination of factors, including variations in patient characteristics, microbiological sampling rates and community antibiotic use. Notably, low rates of stable-state microbiological sampling have been reported in China and parts of Eastern Europe, which may contribute to an underestimation of pathogen prevalence, including S. aureus [ , ]. Impact on inflammatory pathways and clinical features The virulence factors previously described, i.e. adhesins, toxins and biofilm formation, enable S. aureus to persist in the airways of bronchiectasis patients and contribute to disease pathogenesis. However, its relatively low prevalence has historically led clinicians to consider chronic S. aureus infection as a potential indicator of underlying conditions such as allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis or atypical CF/CF transmembrane conductance regulator-related bronchiectasis [ ]. Some evidence is emerging to support the immunoallergic properties of S. aureus in bronchiectasis. A Chinese cohort study demonstrated the highest levels of staphylococcal enterotoxin sensitisation and elevated IgE in individuals with S. aureus infection without concurrent isolation of P. aeruginosa [ ]. Impact on disease progression, lung function, exacerbations, quality of life and mortality The role of S. aureus in bronchiectasis progression remains debated. An analysis from the Spanish RIBRON registry reported that 18% of patients had chronic S. aureus infection, defined as three or more consecutive positive cultures outside of exacerbation periods [ ]. In this cohort, patients with S. aureus were younger, had lower baseline percentage predicted forced expiratory volume in 1 s, exhibited more extensive radiological involvement and experienced more frequent mild-to-moderate exacerbations [ ]. The aforementioned Taiwanese study by C hang et al. [ ], which examined clinical outcomes in adult Asian bronchiectasis patients with MDR bacterial infections, reported a higher risk of both in-hospital and 3-year mortality among individuals with MRSA compared to those without MDR pathogens. Two additional studies explored pathogen burden in adults with bronchiectasis. D ean et al . [ ] conducted a large retrospective cohort study in the USA, reporting a S. aureus isolation rate of 6%, with 15% of these meeting criteria for chronic infection (defined as at least two isolates ≥3 months apart within 1 year). Among 44 patients with chronic S. aureus infection, 50% experienced exacerbations and 82% were hospitalised within 2 years of follow-up, significantly more than in control groups without bacterial isolation. A Chinese study by N iu et al. [ ], focused on hospitalised bronchiectasis patients, found that 28.6% of those with S. aureus infection experienced three or more acute exacerbations during 1-year follow-up. S. aureus was associated with fewer frequent exacerbations compared to P. aeruginosa (50.0%) and Acinetobacter baumannii (66.7%), and lower hospitalisation rates (28.6% versus 58.3% and 100%, respectively). Moreover, univariate Cox regression showed a lower risk of exacerbations with S. aureus (OR 0.363) compared to P. aeruginosa (OR 2.779) and A. baumannii (OR 10.333). Nonetheless, variations in study design and methodology among the aforementioned studies limit generalisability and may partially account for the inconsistencies in findings regarding the impact of S. aureus in bronchiectasis ( ). Additionally, recent data from the EMBARC registry reported that S. aureus infection was associated with younger age and higher rates of co-isolation with other pathogens, but not with worse clinical outcomes such as exacerbations, hospitalisations or mortality [ ]. Treatment recommendations in bronchiectasis Despite increasing evidence on the disease burden associated with S. aureus in bronchiectasis, the latest European Respiratory Society (ERS) guidelines do not offer specific recommendations for the management of this pathogen [ ]. In contrast, the British Thoracic Society guidelines recommend that patients with MRSA isolation be managed in secondary care [ ]. Moreover, if a patient experiences clinical deterioration with a new growth of MRSA, whether as a first isolation or as regrowth following intermittent colonisation, eradication should be considered. However, unlike for P. aeruginosa , for which clear eradication protocols are provided, no standardised MRSA eradication regimen is currently outlined [ , ]. The only formal recommendation available concerns the treatment of S. aureus -related exacerbations. A 14-day course of antibiotics is advised, with oral or intravenous options depending on severity. For MSSA, oral options include amoxicillin–clavulanate or doxycycline; for MRSA, doxycycline, trimethoprim or linezolid are recommended [ ]. Emerging evidence highlights key considerations in antibiotic therapy for bronchiectasis. Impaired mucociliary clearance and structural lung damage may result in high airway bacterial loads [ ]. These conditions can compromise antibiotic efficacy through the so-called inoculum effect, whereby high concentrations of β-lactamase enzymes exert broader hydrolytic activity against β-lactams or overwhelm β-lactamase inhibitors, rendering them less effective [ ]. In practice, broad-spectrum antibiotics such as amoxicillin–clavulanate or piperacillin–tazobactam are often used to treat MSSA-related exacerbations, particularly in hospitalised patients with suspected polymicrobial infections ( e.g. involving P. aeruginosa ). However, recent findings suggest these may not always be the optimal choice. M ossman et al . [ ] demonstrated that β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations, such as piperacillin–tazobactam, are significantly affected by the inoculum effect in bronchiectasis, reducing their efficacy. These findings raise concerns regarding the reliability of β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor agents against S. aureus in high bacterial load settings, suggesting that alternative agents less susceptible to the inoculum effect may be more appropriate in certain cases. Comparison and interaction with other bacteria and viruses In recent years, the role of the airway microbiome and its relationship with bronchiectasis outcomes has gained significant attention [ ]. Patients with bronchiectasis and P. aeruginosa infection tend to experience more severe disease, with poorer quality of life, more frequent exacerbations and higher mortality, compared to those without this infection [ , ]. Although less is known about the clinical impact of other organisms, emerging evidence suggests that H. influenzae , another predominant pathogen, is associated with less severe disease than P. aeruginosa [ ]. Importantly, the isolation of any pathogenic organism appears to increase the risk of both mortality and exacerbations compared to patients in whom no pathogen is ever cultured [ ]. As previously discussed, S. aureus is a highly adaptable bacterium capable of colonising various niches within the human body. Its transition from a commensal organism to a pathogen is influenced by interactions with other microorganisms, including commensal bacteria and respiratory viruses, as well as by its movement from the upper to the lower respiratory tract. Understanding these dynamics is essential to identify the factors that govern S. aureus pathogenicity and to develop novel therapeutic strategies. A key aspect of these interactions is bacterial competition within the microbiota. Certain bacterial species promote S. aureus growth, while others inhibit its proliferation. For instance, anaerobic bacteria in the upper airways, such as Prevotella , Fusobacterium and Streptococcus , can degrade mucins and release metabolites that S. aureus may utilise as energy sources, thereby enhancing its survival and colonisation capacity [ ]. Conversely, other commensal bacteria, including Corynebacterium and Cutibacterium spp., which are present at appreciable relative abundances in the upper airways, have been shown to produce antimicrobial metabolites, such as short-chain fatty acids and porphyrins, that can inhibit S. aureus growth and suppress the expression of its virulence factors; however, the precise concentration thresholds required for these anti-virulence effects have not yet been established [ ]. These interactions support the concept that disease can arise not only from the acquisition of a novel pathogen but also from microbiome imbalance or “dysbiosis”, defined as a decline in beneficial bacteria or reduced microbial diversity, which disrupts homeostasis and facilitates opportunistic infections [ ]. Interactions between P. aeruginosa and S. aureus have been extensively characterised in CF and in in vitro co-culture models, providing much of our current understanding. However, such insights should be extrapolated to bronchiectasis with caution, as this condition presents a more heterogeneous pathophysiology, marked by differences in host immune responses, mucus composition and disease trajectory, that may profoundly influence microbial dynamics. During the course of CF lung disease, P. aeruginosa and S. aureus dynamic interplay evolves over time, showing both competitive and potentially cooperative characteristics [ ]. In early CF, S. aureus is often the first pathogen isolated, and some evidence suggests it may prevent or delay the establishment of P. aeruginosa colonisation [ ]. Conversely, other studies indicate that early S. aureus colonisation may predispose individuals to subsequent P. aeruginosa infection. For example, A lves et al . [ ], in a wound infection model, demonstrated that S. aureus predominated in early biofilms and could serve as a pioneer for P. aeruginosa attachment. As CF progresses, P. aeruginosa typically becomes the dominant pathogen [ ]. In vitro studies have shown that early P. aeruginosa isolates can outcompete S. aureus via mechanisms such as iron sequestration, nutrient competition, reciprocal biofilm disruption and the production of antimicrobial compounds [ , ]. In response to P. aeruginosa 's respiratory inhibition, S. aureus can shift to the SCV phenotype, characterised by a shift to anaerobic metabolism with increased lactate production. Interestingly, this lactate can serve as a carbon source for P. aeruginosa , potentially promoting microbial coexistence in the chronically infected lung [ ]. Clinically, P. aeruginosa – S. aureus co-infection in CF is often associated with worse outcomes compared to mono-infection with either species [ , ]. While these insights can provide useful hypotheses, bronchiectasis-specific studies are urgently needed to validate these findings and guide targeted therapeutic interventions. Beyond bacterial competition, respiratory viruses also play a crucial role in modulating S. aureus pathogenicity. Viral infections, including those caused by rhinovirus, influenza viruses and coronaviruses, can disrupt the microbial equilibrium and create conditions conducive to the overgrowth of opportunistic bacteria, particularly S. aureus and H. influenzae . For instance, influenza infection induces a strong inflammatory response that recruits neutrophils to the lungs. However, S. aureus strains producing PVL can lyse these neutrophils, releasing proteolytic enzymes that exacerbate epithelial damage and promote bacterial dissemination [ ]. For instance, influenza infection induces a strong inflammatory response that recruits neutrophils to the lungs. However, S. aureus strains producing PVL can lyse these neutrophils, releasing proteolytic enzymes that exacerbate epithelial damage and promote bacterial dissemination [ ]. Understanding the complex and often synergistic interplay among S. aureus , P. aeruginosa and other microorganisms in chronic airway diseases is critical to elucidating the cycle of infection, inflammation and pulmonary decline. Prevention Given the significant burden of S. aureus infections, preventive strategies, although largely extrapolated from other clinical contexts, are essential for reducing colonisation, transmission and infection risk. Current approaches rely predominantly on decolonisation measures and rigorous infection control practices, while vaccination remains an area of active investigation, as no effective vaccine is currently available. Infection control guidelines emphasise stringent hygiene protocols, targeted decolonisation in high-risk patients and antibiotic stewardship to limit the spread of resistant strains [ , ]. Most of the available evidence regarding S. aureus prevention originates from studies in acute respiratory conditions, particularly pneumonia, where S. aureus , especially MRSA, represents a major clinical challenge [ ]. Nasal colonisation significantly increases the risk of pneumonia, particularly in hospitalised or immunocompromised patients [ ]. In recent years, the incidence of community-acquired MRSA infections has risen alarmingly, notably affecting paediatric populations and immunocompromised adults. Mortality associated with MRSA pneumonia is markedly higher than with MSSA, with increased risks of sepsis, septic shock and ICU admission [ ]. Necrotising pneumonia, a rare but severe complication of S. aureus infection, is linked to strains that produce PVL toxin, which drives tissue necrosis and a massive inflammatory response [ ]. Despite advances in treatment, mortality rates for this condition range from 20% to >50% [ ]. Therefore, considering the potential for S. aureus to colonise the airways and exacerbate chronic respiratory diseases, preventive strategies in bronchiectasis also warrant consideration. Decolonisation Decolonisation aims to eliminate or suppress S. aureus carriage, as many infections originate from an individual's own colonising strains. S. aureus commonly colonises the nasopharynx, skin and gastrointestinal tract, with ∼1–3% of the general population carrying MRSA. In high-risk individuals, decolonisation strategies can reduce the likelihood of subsequent infection. Nasal decolonisation typically involves the use of mupirocin, an inhibitor of bacterial isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase that disrupts protein synthesis, while skin decolonisation is achieved with antiseptics such as chlorhexidine [ , , ]. Although mupirocin effectively reduces nasal carriage, recolonisation is common and prolonged use may result in resistance. Chlorhexidine is widely employed for skin decolonisation but may cause irritation with repeated application [ , , ]. Overall, evidence suggests that these interventions, used alone or in combination, are effective in reducing S. aureus hospital-acquired infections, including bloodstream infections and ventilator-associated pneumonia, particularly in ICU settings and in patients undergoing high-risk procedures ( e.g. joint replacement and cardiac surgery) or receiving haemodialysis [ , ]. Oral antibiotics are not recommended for routine decolonisation due to the associated risks of antimicrobial resistance and disruption of the gut microbiota. At present, outside of high-risk scenarios, there are no established indications for S. aureus decolonisation, even in chronic respiratory diseases such as bronchiectasis, where S. aureus is frequently isolated from lower airway samples, often during stable phases of disease. Vaccines The development of a vaccine against S. aureus presents significant challenges, primarily due to the complexity of the human immune response to this pathogen's unique characteristics. A major obstacle is the limited understanding of the immune mechanisms required for protection against S. aureus . Although numerous vaccine candidates targeting surface antigens have successfully generated opsonising antibody responses in animal models, they have failed to demonstrate efficacy in human clinical trials [ ]. This highlights the inadequacy of humoral immunity alone, particularly opsonophagocytic activity, as a protective mechanism in humans. Findings from genetic and acquired immunodeficiency syndromes that predispose to S. aureus infections suggest that cell-mediated immunity plays a central role in host defence. Components such as T-cells, dendritic cells and macrophages, particularly those within the T-helper cell 17–neutrophil axis, are crucial in containing S. aureus [ ]. Conditions that impair these mechanisms, including prolonged corticosteroid therapy and vitamin D deficiency, are associated with increased susceptibility. These insights suggest that future vaccines may need to induce robust cellular responses in addition to humoral immunity to achieve effective protection. Novel approaches Innovative strategies are currently under investigation to address the limitations of current decolonisation methods and the challenges faced in vaccine development, with the goal of preserving microbiome integrity and minimising antibiotic resistance [ ]. For example, suvratoxumab, a monoclonal antibody targeting the S. aureus α-toxin, has been evaluated for the prevention of ventilator-associated pneumonia in ICU

These insights suggest that future vaccines may need to induce robust cellular responses in addition to humoral immunity to achieve effective protection. Novel approaches Innovative strategies are currently under investigation to address the limitations of current decolonisation methods and the challenges faced in vaccine development, with the goal of preserving microbiome integrity and minimising antibiotic resistance [ ]. For example, suvratoxumab, a monoclonal antibody targeting the S. aureus α-toxin, has been evaluated for the prevention of ventilator-associated pneumonia in ICU patients. A phase 2 pilot trial of suvratoxumab demonstrated a non-statistically significant reduction in the incidence of S. aureus pneumonia at 30 days; however, the findings support monoclonal antibody therapy as a promising, safe and feasible option for pre-emptive treatment against staphylococcal infections [ ]. Larger studies are needed to further evaluate the efficacy and potential role of this and other emerging approaches in reducing the burden of S. aureus infections. Questions for future research and points for clinical practice S. aureus is increasingly recognised as a relevant pathogen in bronchiectasis, although its epidemiological significance and clinical impact remain less prominent compared to other microorganisms, particularly P. aeruginosa . While some studies have reported an association between S. aureus and worse lung function, more extensive radiological disease and increased exacerbation frequency, others interpret its presence as a marker of underlying disease severity rather than a direct contributor to disease progression ( ). Currently, there is insufficient evidence to support specific recommendations for the routine management of S. aureus in bronchiectasis. Existing guidelines advise that MRSA-positive patients be monitored in secondary care, with eradication considered in cases of clinical deterioration; however, no standardised eradication protocol has been established. In contrast, S. aureus -related exacerbations should be treated with a 14-day course of an appropriate antibiotic ( ). Several key questions remain unanswered. These include the true pathogenic role of S. aureus in bronchiectasis, its contribution to disease trajectory, and the prevalence and clinical implications of co-infection with other pathogens. Further research is also needed to elucidate the effects of S. aureus on airway inflammation, microbiota composition and immune responses in the context of bronchiectasis ( ). Moreover, the potential utility of decolonisation strategies, already implemented in other disease models, has yet to be evaluated in chronic respiratory diseases such as bronchiectasis. Finally, novel interventions including vaccines and monoclonal antibody therapies are either under active investigation or merit further exploration as potential therapeutic tools in this setting.
